ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Xiaoming has designed a game where a frog catches a fly. Both the frog and the fly move within a vertical $xOy$ plane. The fly starts from rest at any position on the horizontal $x$-axis and undergoes uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion with a constant acceleration of magnitude $\frac{5}{9}g$ ($g$ is the acceleration due to gravity). The acceleration is always directed $37^{\circ}$ upward relative to the negative $x$-axis (the positive direction of the $x$-axis is to the right). The frog is located at point $M$ on the $y$-axis, with $OM=H$. It can jump horizontally to the right or left at different speeds, subject only to gravity during its motion. Both the frog and the fly are treated as point masses, and $\sin37^{\circ}=\frac{3}{5}$ is given.

1. After the fly has been in motion for some time, the frog jumps horizontally to the right at its maximum jumping speed and catches the fly at a height of $y=\frac{3}{4}H$. Given that the ratio of the frog's horizontal displacement to the fly's horizontal displacement is $2{\sqrt{2}}:3$, determine the maximum jumping speed of the frog.
2. If the frog's jumping speed is no greater than the maximum jumping speed found in question (1), and the frog jumps no earlier than the fly starts moving, and the fly can be caught, determine the range of positions on the $x$-axis from which the fly can emerge.
3. If the fly takes off from a certain position, the frog can choose to jump at a certain moment with a certain speed, such that the ratio of the frog's movement time to the fly's movement time is $1 : \sqrt{2}$. Alternatively, the frog can choose to jump at another moment with the same speed, such that the ratio of the frog's movement time to the fly's movement time is $1 : \sqrt{17}$. Determine all possible positions from which the fly can take off and the corresponding jump speed of the frog.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Solve according to the specified absolute-coordinate kinematics method. First decompose the fly's acceleration: the acceleration magnitude is (5/9)g, the direction is 37° upward relative to the negative x-axis, and sin37°=3/5, cos37°=4/5, so a_x=-(5/9)g·(4/5)=-(4/9)g, a_y=(5/9)g·(3/5)=(1/3)g. Suppose the fly starts from rest at (x0,0), and the total motion time is T, then at the time of capture the fly's coordinates are x_f=x0-(2/9)gT^2, y_f=(1/6)gT^2. Suppose the frog delays for a period of time after the fly starts and then jumps, the frog's own flight time is t, and the horizontal initial velocity is the signed quantity u, then at the time of capture the frog's coordinates are x_F=ut, y_F=H-(1/2)gt^2. Capture requires the two coordinates to be equal. The vertical direction gives H-(1/2)gt^2=(1/6)gT^2, that is T^2+3t^2=6H/g. The frog does not jump earlier than the fly, so 0<t≤T. 1. Capture height y=3H/4. From the fly's vertical coordinate: (1/6)gT^2=3H/4, obtaining T^2=9H/(2g). From the frog's vertical coordinate: H-(1/2)gt^2=3H/4, obtaining t^2=H/(2g). Therefore t=T/3. At this time the magnitude of the fly's horizontal displacement is (2/9)gT^2=(2/9)g·9H/(2g)=H. The problem gives frog horizontal displacement : fly horizontal displacement =2√2:3, therefore the frog's horizontal displacement is ut=(2√2/3)H. Therefore the frog's maximum jump speed v_m=u=(ut)/t=(2√2H/3)/sqrt(H/(2g))=(4/3)sqrt(gH). 2. Let r=t/T, 0<r≤1. From T^2+3t^2=6H/g, obtain T^2=6H/[g(1+3r^2)]. The horizontal direction satisfies ut=x0-(2/9)gT^2, so x0/H=4/[3(1+3r^2)] +(u/sqrt(gH))·r·sqrt(6/(1+3r^2)). Denote A(r)=4/[3(1+3r^2)], B(r)=r sqrt(6/(1+3r^2)). From question 1, |u|≤v_m=(4/3)sqrt(gH), therefore for fixed r, x0/H ∈ [A(r)-(4/3)B(r), A(r)+(4/3)B(r)]. Examine the upper-end function f_+(r)=A(r)+(4/3)B(r). Its derivative is f_+'(r)=-8r/(1+3r^2)^2 +(4/3)√6/(1+3r^2)^(3/2). Set the derivative to 0, obtaining r=1/√3, and at this time f_+(1/√3)=2. Examine the lower-end function f_-(r)=A(r)-(4/3)B(r), its derivative f_-'(r)=-8r/(1+3r^2)^2 -(4/3)√6/(1+3r^2)^(3/2)<0, therefore it is monotonically decreasing on 0<r≤1, and the minimum value is obtained at r=1: f_-(1)=1/3-(4/3)(√6/2)=(1-2√6)/3. These intervals are mutually connected, therefore the range of the fly's starting point is [(1-2√6)H/3, 2H]. 3. For the same starting point x0, let s=x0/H. From the formula in question 2, the dimensionless quantity of the signed velocity required for a given r is q(r,s)=u/sqrt(gH)=[s-A(r)]/B(r). The time ratios of the two schemes in the problem are frog time : fly time =1:√2 and 1:√17, that is r1=t/T=1/√2, r2=1/√17. When r1=1/√2, A1=4/[3(1+3/2)]=8/15, B1=(1/√2)sqrt(6/(5/2))=sqrt(6/5). When r2=1/√17, A2=4/[3(1+3/17)]=17/15, B2=(1/√17)sqrt(6/(20/17))=sqrt(3/10). The two jump speeds are the same, and the directions may be the same or opposite, therefore it is required that |q(r1,s)|=|q(r2,s)|, that is (s-8/15)^2/(6/5)=(s-17/15)^2/(3/10). Simplifying gives (s-8/15)^2=4(s-17/15)^2. Thus s-8/15=2(s-17/15) or s-8/15=-2(s-17/15). The first gives s=26/15; at this time |q|=(26/15-8/15)/sqrt(6/5)=sqrt(30)/5, so v=(1/5)sqrt(30gH). The second gives s=14/15; at this time |q|=(14/15-8/15)/sqrt(6/5)=sqrt(30)/15, so v=(1/15)sqrt(30gH).

 x_F=ut, y_F=H-(1/2)gt^2.
Capture requires the two coordinates to be equal. The vertical direction gives

that is
 T^2+3t^2=6H/g.
The frog does not jump earlier than the fly, so 0<t≤T.

1. Capture height y=3H/4. From the fly's vertical coordinate:
 (1/6)gT^2=3H/4, obtaining T^2=9H/(2g).
From the frog's vertical coordinate:

Therefore t=T/3.
At this time the magnitude of the fly's horizontal displacement is

The problem gives frog horizontal displacement : fly horizontal displacement =2√2:3, therefore the frog's horizontal displacement is
 ut=(2√2/3)H.
Therefore the frog's maximum jump speed
 v_m=u=(ut)/t=(2√2H/3)/sqrt(H/(2g))=(4/3)sqrt(gH).

2. Let r=t/T, 0<r≤1. From T^2+3t^2=6H/g, obtain
 T^2=6H/[g(1+3r^2)].
The horizontal direction satisfies

so
 x0/H=4/[3(1+3r^2)] +(u/sqrt(gH))·r·sqrt(6/(1+3r^2)).
